docs.text: HardFOC driver MCP9700 Driver ¶ A C++17 driver for the Microchip MCP9700, MCP9700A and MCP9700B linear active thermistors. It reads the sensor's output voltage through your ADC and returns degrees Celsius, with the datasheet coefficients or your own calibration, on any MCU with an ADC input. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that brings your ADC up and returns the voltage at the sensor's output pin; it does the rest: the transfer function, the coefficients and the error checks around each read. Linear active thermistor (analog temperature sensor) MCP9700 / MCP9700A Microchip Technology Function Temperature to voltage: 500 mV at 0 °C, 10.0 mV/°C (typical) Output VOUT 100 mV to 1.75 V over the range; 100 µA maximum; drives capacitive loads Supply 2.3 V to 5.5 V, 6 µA typical (12 µA maximum) Accuracy (0 °C to +70 °C) MCP9700 ±4 °C, MCP9700A ±2 °C maximum; MCP9700B ±1 °C from +20 °C to +70 °C Range −40 °C to +125 °C; to +150 °C for the high-temperature MCP9700 and MCP9700B (SOT-23, SC70) Package SOT-23-3, SC70-5, TO-92-3 (no TO-92 for the MCP9700B) Driver mode One ADC read per call, first-order transfer function with configurable coefficients Datasheet (DS20001942L) · MCP9700 product page · MCP9700A product page What you get ¶ One object per sensor. Mcp9700Thermistor<YourAdc> takes your ADC adapter and a channel; several sensors share one ADC. See API guide . Degrees Celsius from volts. ReadTemperatureCelsius() applies T = (V − 0.5 V) / 0.01 V/°C , the datasheet's first-order transfer function. See Transfer function . Your calibration. Pass your own offset and slope to the constructor after a one-point or two-point calibration, or the MCP9701 coefficients. See Configuration . Errors you can act on. Every call returns bool and LastError() says why; an open, grounded or shorted input fails instead of reading −50 °C. A failed read leaves your value untouched. See API guide . Zero-overhead portability. The adapter is a template parameter with two methods: no virtual calls, no heap, no RTOS dependency. See Porting . Tested without hardware. Host unit tests run the driver against a scripted ADC. See Testing and CI . Where to go next ¶ Quickstart Wire the sensor, write the adapter, print the temperature in about 15 lines. API guide ¶ How to do the common jobs with the driver: construct, initialise, read, average and handle errors. Every snippet on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/api_tasks.cpp , with Sensor standing for hf::mcp9700::Mcp9700Thermistor<MyAdc> . The API reference lists every member. The shape of the API ¶ One Mcp9700Thermistor<AdcType> object per sensor, in namespace hf::mcp9700 . Member What it does Constructor Stores the adapter, channel and coefficients; no ADC access Initialize() Checks the arguments, calls the adapter's EnsureInitialized() ReadTemperatureCelsius(float*) One ADC read, converted to °C and checked against the sensor's range ReadVoltage(float*) One ADC read, the raw VOUT in volts: no conversion, no range check SetSpecifiedRange(min, max, margin) The temperature range a reading must fall in (default −40 °C to +125 °C, 8 °C margin) LastError() Why the last call that can fail failed ( hf::mcp9700::Error ) Deinitialize() Marks the object uninitialised; reads fail until Initialize() VoltsAtZeroC() The offset in use VoltsPerCelsius() The slope in use HasValidCoefficients() true when the offset is finite and the slope is finite and above zero GetMcp9700DriverVersion() The version string (free function) Every call is noexcept and never throws. The calls that can fail return bool : check it. Construct and initialise ¶ Sensor board ( & adc , 0 ); // MCP9700 / 9700A / 9700B: datasheet typicals Sensor trimmed ( & adc , 1 , 0.4962F , 0.01003F ); // per-unit coefficients from a calibration return board . Initialize () && trimmed . Initialize (); The two coefficient arguments are optional. Leave them out for the MCP9700, MCP9700A and MCP9700B datasheet typicals; pass your own after a calibration ( Configuration ). The channel is passed to your adapter unchanged: it means whatever your adapter says it means. Initialize() returns false when the adapter pointer is null, when the coefficients are unusable ( v_per_c zero, negative, NaN or infinite, or v_zero_c NaN or infinite), or when EnsureInitialized() returns false . Several sensors can share one adapter; each Initialize() calls EnsureInitialized() again, so make it safe to call twice. Read the temperature ¶ float celsius = 0.0F ; if ( ! sensor . ReadTemperatureCelsius ( & celsius )) { return false ; // celsius is unchanged on failure } std :: printf ( "%.2f C (V0 = %.4f V, Tc = %.5f V/C) 
 " , static_cast < double > ( celsius ), static_cast < double > ( sensor . VoltsAtZeroC ()), static_cast < double > ( sensor . VoltsPerCelsius ())); return true ; Each call is one ReadChannelV() call. The driver keeps no history and no cache. Average several reads ¶ constexpr int kSamples = 16 ; float sum = 0.0F ; for ( int i = 0 ; i < kSamples ; ++ i ) { float t = 0.0F ; if ( ! sensor . ReadTemperatureCelsius ( & t )) { return false ; } sum += t ; } * celsius = sum / static_cast < float > ( kSamples ); return true ; The sensor's thermal response is about a second ( Hardware ), so averaging a burst of reads filters ADC and supply noise without hiding real temperature changes. Handle errors ¶ float t = 0.0F ; if ( ! sensor . ReadTemperatureCelsius ( & t )) { switch ( sensor . LastError ()) { case hf :: mcp9700 :: Error :: kOutOfRange : { // open, grounded or shorted input, or wrong ADC scale float volts = 0.0F ; if ( sensor . ReadVoltage ( & volts )) { // the raw VOUT, unconverted and unchecked std :: printf ( "VOUT %.3f V is outside the sensor's range 
 " , static_cast < double > ( volts )); } break ; } case hf :: mcp9700 :: Error :: kAdcError : // ReadChannelV() returned non-zero std :: printf ( "ADC read failed 
 " ); break ; default : // not initialised or null output break ; } return false ; // t is unchanged on failure } * celsius = t ; return true ; LastError() Meaning Error::kInvalidArgument Null adapter, null output pointer, or an invalid range passed to SetSpecifiedRange() Error::kInvalidCoefficients Initialize() : the slope is not a finite positive number, or the offset is not finite Error::kAdcError Your EnsureInitialized() returned false or your ReadChannelV() returned non-zero Error::kNotInitialized Read before a successful Initialize() , or after Deinitialize() Error::kOutOfRange The temperature is outside the specified range plus the margin, or not a number Error::kNone The last call succeeded kOutOfRange catches the faults a plain conversion would report as a temperature: VOUT at 0 V (open wire, grounded input or unpowered sensor, which would read −50 °C), VOUT near the supply, or an adapter that returns millivolts. A working MCP9700 outputs 100 mV to 1.75 V over −40 °C to +125 °C (datasheet Section 3.2); with the 8 °C margin the driver accepts 20 mV to 1.83 V. A floating input that happens to settle inside that window cannot be told from a temperature. On a failed read the output value is not written. ReadVoltage() returns the raw VOUT without the range check, to see what the pin reads. Set the plausible range ¶ // High-temperature MCP9700 / MCP9700B (SOT-23-3, SC70-5): specified to +150 C. Keep the 8 C margin. return sensor . SetSpecifiedRange ( -40.0F , 150.0F ); The default range is the MCP9700 family's specified range. Widen it to +150 °C for the high-temperature parts, narrow it to −10 °C for the MCP9701 ( Configuration ). The margin (default kDefaultRangeMarginCelsius , 8 °C) covers the sensor's worst-case accuracy limits (−4 °C / +6 °C for the MCP9700) and some ADC error. Re-initialise and read the version ¶ sensor . Deinitialize (); // reads now fail; the ADC itself stays as it is if ( ! sensor . Initialize ()) { // calls EnsureInitialized() again std :: printf ( "ADC did not come back 
 " ); } std :: printf ( "driver %s 
 " , GetMcp9700DriverVersion ()); Deinitialize() only changes the driver's state; shutting down the ADC is your adapter's job. Next ¶ Configuration for calibration; Porting for the adapter contract.

docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is put together: three layers, what each owns, and how one read reaches the sensor. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one Mcp9700Thermistor object per sensor, whose public calls (listed from inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp) initialise the ADC and return degrees Celsius. The core turns one ADC voltage into a temperature with (V - v_zero_c) / v_per_c. The ADC adapter contract is the template parameter: any class with the two methods named in the header's documentation, checked at compile time. The platform port is the only code you write: that class, which brings your ADC up and returns the voltage at the sensor's VOUT pin. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp Mcp9700Thermistor public calls ; inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp AdcType contract ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . The three layers ¶ Layer What it is Changes Core Mcp9700Thermistor<AdcType> Never, for a new board Adapter contract The AdcType parameter Never Platform adapter Your class, two methods Once per MCU ( Porting ) The core is in inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp and src/mcp9700_thermistor.ipp ; the contract is documented on the class in the same header. Everything above the adapter is the same on ESP32, STM32, a Linux host or the unit-test mock. That is how the host tests run the real driver code without hardware. How one read reaches the sensor ¶ sequenceDiagram participant A as Application participant D as Mcp9700Thermistor participant P as Your adapter participant H as ADC and MCP9700 A->>D: ReadTemperatureCelsius(&t) D->>D: initialised? output pointer not null? D->>P: ReadChannelV(channel, &volts) P->>H: one conversion on VOUT H-->>P: raw code P-->>D: 0 and volts (calibrated, at the pin) D->>D: t = (volts − v_zero_c) / v_per_c D-->>A: true (on a non-zero return: false, t unchanged) Why a template parameter ¶ The adapter is a class template parameter, not a virtual base class. The compiler sees your adapter's methods directly and inlines them; the driver has no vtable, allocates nothing and needs no RTTI. There is no base class to derive from either: any type with the two methods compiles, and a type without them fails to compile where the driver calls them. The cost is that the driver type names the adapter: Mcp9700Thermistor<MyAdc> . What the driver owns and what it does not ¶ The driver Your adapter or application The transfer function and its two coefficients ADC set-up, channel mapping, calibration, dividers The initialised state, the argument checks and the plausibility range check Averaging, filtering, application limits Returning false on any failure Deciding what a failure means for your system The driver holds a non-owning pointer to your adapter: the adapter must outlive it. The object cannot be copied. The constructor never touches the ADC; Initialize() does, through EnsureInitialized() . docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries marked BREAKING need source changes in code that used the affected API. Unreleased ¶ Breaking changes ¶ BREAKING ReadTemperatureCelsius() now fails (returns false , output untouched) when the converted temperature is outside the specified range plus a margin, by default −40 °C to +125 °C ± 8 °C (20 mV to 1.83 V). An open or grounded input (0 V) used to return −50 °C as a successful read. Code that reads a high-temperature MCP9700/MCP9700B above +133 °C must call SetSpecifiedRange(-40.0F, 150.0F) . MCP9701 users should call SetSpecifiedRange(-10.0F, 125.0F) : with the MCP9701 coefficients 0 V is −20.5 °C, inside the default window. Documentation ¶ The documentation site moved to the HardFOC MkDocs platform: new page set (quickstart, hardware, transfer function, architecture, API guide, configuration, porting, examples, troubleshooting), the Doxygen API reference under /api/ , and every code sample compiled by the host build from tests/docs/ . Corrected the hardware facts: the accuracy limits are ±4 °C (MCP9700) and ±2 °C (MCP9700A) maximum from 0 °C to +70 °C, not ±2 °C and ±1 °C typical; the output is not ratiometric to VDD; the README no longer lists a ReadVoltage() call that did not exist then. Fixed ¶ HF_MCP9700_ENABLE_WARNINGS no longer adds -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic as INTERFACE options of hf::mcp9700 , which changed the warning flags of every target that linked the driver. The option is deprecated and has no effect; it prints a deprecation message when set. Add warnings to your own target instead. Initialize() now rejects a NaN or infinite slope or offset ( Error::kInvalidCoefficients ). Before, only a slope of zero or below was caught, and a NaN or infinite coefficient made every reading NaN, 0 or infinite. Added ¶ CMake install rules: cmake --install copies the header, the .ipp and the generated mcp9700_version.h under include/hf_mcp9700/ , and a package configuration, so find_package(hf_mcp9700) provides hf::mcp9700 . The package configuration used to include the build-settings file, which is not installed. ReadVoltage(float*) : the raw sensor output voltage, without conversion or range check. Plausibility range check on ReadTemperatureCelsius() , configurable with SetSpecifiedRange() ; kDefaultSpecifiedMinCelsius , kDefaultSpecifiedMaxCelsius , kDefaultRangeMarginCelsius . hf::mcp9700::Error and LastError() : why the last call failed. HasValidCoefficients() : whether the offset and slope can be used. Host unit tests ( HF_MCP9700_BUILD_TESTS ) that run the driver against a scripted ADC adapter.

docs.text: Configuration ¶ The two coefficients the driver uses, where their values come from, and how to calibrate them for one sensor. The driver has no configuration structure and no registers: the constructor's two coefficient arguments and the plausibility range are the whole configuration. Snippets are compiled from tests/docs/configuration.cpp . Constructor arguments ¶ Argument Default Meaning adc_interface AdcType* : your adapter; must outlive the driver adc_channel uint8_t : passed to ReadChannelV() unchanged v_zero_c 0.5F Output at 0 °C, in volts v_per_c 0.01F Slope in volts per °C; must be finite and greater than 0 The coefficients cannot be changed after construction. VoltsAtZeroC() and VoltsPerCelsius() read them back. Datasheet values ¶ Part v_zero_c (V) v_per_c (V/°C) MCP9700, MCP9700A, MCP9700B 0.500 0.0100 MCP9701, MCP9701A 0.400 0.0195 These are typical values from the DC Electrical Characteristics; the datasheet gives no minimum or maximum for them. The spread between parts is in the accuracy limits instead ( Hardware ). One-point calibration ¶ Measure VOUT once at a known temperature, keep the typical slope and move the offset. At +25 °C this gives ±0.5 °C typical from 0 °C to +70 °C (datasheet Section 4.1). // One-point calibration: keep the 10 mV/°C slope, move the offset so the sensor reads the reference. // Measured: VOUT = 0.7431 V while a reference thermometer next to it reads 24.6 °C. constexpr float kSlope = hf :: mcp9700 :: kDefaultVoltsPerCelsius ; constexpr float kOffset = 0.7431F - kSlope * 24.6F ; // 0.4971 V at 0 °C Read the voltage with the same ADC and adapter you will use in operation, so the ADC's offset is calibrated out too. Let the sensor and the reference settle at the same temperature first. Two-point calibration ¶ Measure VOUT at two temperatures far apart, for example 0 °C and +70 °C, and fit both coefficients. struct Coefficients { float v_zero_c ; // volts at 0 °C float v_per_c ; // volts per °C }; // Two-point calibration: VOUT measured at two reference temperatures far apart (here 0 °C and +70 °C). constexpr Coefficients two_point ( float t1_c , float v1 , float t2_c , float v2 ) { const float slope = ( v2 - v1 ) / ( t2_c - t1_c ); return { v1 - slope * t1_c , slope }; } constexpr Coefficients kUnit7 = two_point ( 0.0F , 0.4987F , 70.0F , 1.2034F ); This also corrects the ADC's gain error. It cannot correct the sensor's nonlinearity (±0.5 °C typical over 0 °C to +70 °C), which remains between and outside the two points. Apply the coefficients ¶ hf :: mcp9700 :: Mcp9700Thermistor < MyAdc > one_point ( & adc , 0 , kOffset , kSlope ); hf :: mcp9700 :: Mcp9700Thermistor < MyAdc > two_point_sensor ( & adc , 1 , kUnit7 . v_zero_c , kUnit7 . v_per_c ); Store the coefficients per unit (non-volatile memory, a calibration table) and pass them at construction. Other parts of the family ¶ // MCP9701 / MCP9701A: same transfer function, different typicals (datasheet DC characteristics). constexpr float kMcp9701VoltsAtZeroC = 0.400F ; // 400 mV constexpr float kMcp9701VoltsPerCelsius = 0.0195F ; // 19.5 mV/°C constexpr float kMcp9701MinCelsius = -10.0F ; // specified range -10 °C to +125 °C constexpr float kMcp9701MaxCelsius = 125.0F ; bool make_mcp9701 ( MyAdc & adc ) { hf :: mcp9700 :: Mcp9700Thermistor < MyAdc > sensor ( & adc , 2 , kMcp9701VoltsAtZeroC , kMcp9701VoltsPerCelsius ); return sensor . SetSpecifiedRange ( kMcp9701MinCelsius , kMcp9701MaxCelsius ) && sensor . Initialize (); } The MCP9701 and MCP9701A use the same equation with these typicals, a 3.1 V to 5.5 V supply and an output of 200 mV to 3 V, specified from −10 °C to +125 °C, so the snippet narrows the plausibility range as well. The driver was written and tested for the MCP9700 family; with these coefficients it computes the MCP9701 transfer function the same way. Plausibility range ¶ ReadTemperatureCelsius() fails with Error::kOutOfRange when the result is outside the specified temperature range widened by a margin on both sides ( API guide ). Set it with SetSpecifiedRange(min_celsius, max_celsius, margin_celsius) . Part min_celsius max_celsius Datasheet MCP9700, MCP9700A, MCP9700B (default) −40 +125 Temperature Characteristics, specified range MCP9700, MCP9700B high temperature (SOT-23-3, SC70-5) −40 +150 Temperature Characteristics MCP9701, MCP9701A −10 +125 Temperature Characteristics The margin defaults to 8 °C ( kDefaultRangeMarginCelsius ). It must be zero or more; a minimum that is not below the maximum, or a value that is not finite, is refused and the previous range is kept. docs.text: Hardware ¶ What to connect between your MCU and an MCP9700, how to set up the ADC, and what limits the accuracy. All values here come from the MCP970X family datasheet (DS20001942L, 2005-2024); section and table names refer to it. The repository does not ship the PDF. Values marked derived are calculated from the datasheet, not taken from it. Pins ¶ Signal SOT-23, TO-92 SC70-5 VDD: supply 1 4 VOUT: output 2 3 GND: ground 3 2 NC 1, 5 The SC70 NC pins are not connected to the die. Tie them to a copper trace from the heat source you measure for better thermal contact. Source: Table 3-1. The TO-92 numbering is in the bottom view of the package drawing; check your part's drawing before you solder. Wiring ¶ Connect VDD to a 2.3 V to 5.5 V rail, GND to the ADC's ground and VOUT straight to an ADC input. The sensor needs no other parts (Section 4.3). Put the decoupling capacitor close to VDD and GND, use a ceramic one, and keep digital lines away from the sensor. Situation Recommendation Normal board 0.1 µF to 1 µF between VDD and GND Noisy supply Feed VDD through a 200 Ω resistor, with 1 µF to GND Powered from an MCU pin Decoupling capacitor and series resistor against the pin's switching noise (Section 4.2) The series resistor goes in the supply line. The datasheet asks for nothing in series with VOUT. Output characteristics ¶ Parameter Value V 0°C , output at 0 °C 500 mV typical T C , coefficient 10.0 mV/°C typical Output range, −40 °C to +125 °C 100 mV to 1.75 V Nonlinearity, 0 °C to +70 °C ±0.5 °C typical Output current 100 µA maximum Output impedance 20 Ω typical (100 µA, 500 Hz) Load capacitance 1000 pF, as characterised Line regulation 0.1 °C/V typical The first two rows are the driver's defaults, kDefaultVoltsAtZeroC and kDefaultVoltsPerCelsius . The output range is from Section 3.2; the driver rejects readings well outside it as an open, grounded or shorted input ( Configuration ). The sensor is characterised and tested with 1000 pF on VOUT; it does not need the capacitor to be stable. The output is not ratiometric: a 3.3 V and a 5 V supply give the same voltage at the same temperature, within the line regulation. The datasheet says added capacitance on VOUT reduces overshoot and undershoot, and that the sensor can sit far from the MCU because it is immune to parasitic capacitance. ADC settings ¶ The driver needs volts at VOUT. Set the ADC so that: The full scale reaches 1.75 V. Use the smallest range or attenuation that still covers it, to keep the most codes per degree. The reading is calibrated. Apply your MCU's ADC calibration in the adapter; the ADC's own offset and gain error adds to the sensor's. Dividers are undone. If VOUT goes through a divider or buffer with gain, the adapter scales back to the pin voltage. ADC 1 LSB Resolution 8-bit, 2.5 V reference 9.8 mV About 1 °C per code (datasheet) 10-bit, 3.3 V reference 3.2 mV 0.32 °C per code (derived) 12-bit, 3.3 V reference 0.81 mV 0.08 °C per code (derived) 12-bit, 4.096 V reference 1.0 mV 0.1 °C per code (datasheet) A finer ADC does not make the sensor more accurate; it lets you see small changes. See Transfer function for the error budget. Timing ¶ Parameter Typical Turn-on time, t ON 800 µs Thermal response to 63 %, SC70-5 on a 1 in × 1 in copper board 1.3 s Thermal response to 63 %, TO-92-3 leaded, without a board 1.65 s The thermal response is measured from air at 30 °C into a fluid bath at +125 °C. The turn-on time matters when you power the sensor from an MCU pin: wait before the first read. The datasheet gives no maximum turn-on time; leave margin. Reading faster than the thermal response does not follow temperature faster; average instead ( API guide ). sequenceDiagram participant M as MCU participant S as MCP9700 M->>S: drive the supply pin high (sensor powered from GPIO) Note over S: t_ON, 800 µs typical M->>S: ADC conversion on VOUT S-->>M: volts M->>M: ReadTemperatureCelsius(): (V − 0.5) / 0.01 M->>S: drive the supply pin low Accuracy ¶ Part 0 °C to +70 °C −40 °C to +125 °C MCP9700 ±4.0 °C −4.0 °C to +6.0 °C MCP9700A ±2.0 °C −2.0 °C to +4.0 °C MCP9700B ±1.0 °C (+20 °C to +70 °C) −2.0 °C to +4.0 °C Limits are minimum and maximum, tested at VDD = 3.3 V, with the first-order equation (DC Electrical Characteristics). A one-point calibration at +25 °C gives ±0.5 °C typical from 0 °C to +70 °C (Section 4.1); see Configuration . The sensor measures the temperature of its die, which follows the board through the pins more than the air around it (Section 4.4). Use the TO-92 package to measure air temperature. Self-heating is small: 0.179 °C in the datasheet's worst case (5.5 V, 12 µA, 100 µA output load, SC70). docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake or ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++17 library with no dependencies. Requirements ¶ A C++17 compiler. CI builds with GCC and Clang on Ubuntu 24.04, and with the ESP-IDF toolchain. CMake 3.16 or newer, which also generates the version header. No RTOS, heap or exceptions: every call is noexcept and returns bool or a value. Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to a version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-mcp9700-driver.git external/hf-mcp9700-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-mcp9700-driver Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples have their own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ); you do not need it to use the driver. CMake ¶ add_subdirectory ( external/hf-mcp9700-driver ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf::mcp9700 ) hf::mcp9700 is an alias of the hf_mcp9700 INTERFACE target. It carries both include directories ( inc/ and the generated mcp9700_version.h ) and requires C++17 ( cxx_std_17 ), so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect HF_MCP9700_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF Deprecated, no effect (prints a deprecation message). Set warnings on your own target HF_MCP9700_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host unit tests in tests/ ( Testing and CI ) Install and find_package ¶ cmake --install copies the header, the .ipp , the generated mcp9700_version.h and a package configuration: cmake -S external/hf-mcp9700-driver -B build-mcp9700 cmake --install build-mcp9700 --prefix /opt/hardfoc Installed path Contents include/hf_mcp9700/inc/ mcp9700_thermistor.hpp , mcp9700_version.h include/hf_mcp9700/src/ mcp9700_thermistor.ipp , included by the header as ../src/ lib/cmake/hf_mcp9700/ hf_mcp9700Config.cmake , hf_mcp9700ConfigVersion.cmake , hf_mcp9700Targets.cmake A consumer then finds the same hf::mcp9700 target. docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the ADC adapter. The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls two methods on the class you pass as the AdcType template parameter (documented on Mcp9700Thermistor in inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp ). There is no base class: the calls are resolved at compile time, so there are no virtual functions, no vtable and nothing to allocate. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one Mcp9700Thermistor object per sensor, whose public calls (listed from inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp) initialise the ADC and return degrees Celsius. The core turns one ADC voltage into a temperature with (V - v_zero_c) / v_per_c. The ADC adapter contract is the template parameter: any class with the two methods named in the header's documentation, checked at compile time. The platform port is the only code you write: that class, which brings your ADC up and returns the voltage at the sensor's VOUT pin. Below it is the hardware. Drawn from: inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp Mcp9700Thermistor public calls ; inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp AdcType contract ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . What you implement ¶ Both are noexcept ; the adapter below shows the exact signatures. Method Contract EnsureInitialized() Bring the ADC up; return true when it can read. Called by every Initialize() ReadChannelV() One reading of channel , in volts at the sensor pin, into *voltage_v ; return 0 on success, anything else on failure ReadChannelV() returns an int where 0 is success, so an adapter can return the value of an error enum whose success value is 0. The driver only tests it against zero. The adapter ¶ my_adc.hpp class MyAdc { public : // Bring the ADC up. The driver calls this from Initialize(); return true when it is ready. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_adc_init (); } return ready_ ; } // Volts at the MCP9700 VOUT pin. Return 0 on success, any other value on failure. int ReadChannelV ( uint8_t channel , float * voltage_v ) noexcept { int32_t mv = 0 ; if ( ! ready_ || ! platform_adc_read_mv ( channel , & mv )) { return 1 ; } * voltage_v = static_cast < float > ( mv ) / 1000.0F ; return 0 ; } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Rules the adapter must follow: Volts, at the pin. Not millivolts, not raw codes. Undo any divider, attenuator or amplifier gain. Calibrated. Apply your ADC's calibration (offset, gain, curve) before returning. Idempotent initialisation. EnsureInitialized() may be called once per sensor and again after Deinitialize() ; set the ADC up only the first time. Fail loudly. Return non-zero when the conversion fails or the channel is unknown; the driver then leaves the caller's value untouched. Do not write *voltage_v on failure. One channel, one sensor. The channel number is yours to define: an ADC channel, a multiplexer input or an index into a table. Reference implementation ¶ The ESP32-C6 example's Esp32Mcp9700Adc in mcp9700_esp32c6_example.cpp is a complete adapter over ESP-IDF adc_oneshot : ADC_UNIT_1 , ADC_CHANNEL_0 (GPIO0), 12-bit, with curve-fitting calibration when the chip supports it. Start from it for any ESP-IDF target. Check your adapter ¶ Build it: the adapter on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/my_adc.hpp , with the driver instantiated over it. Measure VOUT with a multimeter and compare it with what ReadChannelV() returns. They should agree within your ADC's error. At room temperature, ReadTemperatureCelsius() should report roughly +20 °C to +30 °C (VOUT about 0.7 V to 0.8 V). Touch the sensor: the reading should rise within a few seconds. Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each sensor one owner task, or guard every call on a driver object (and its adapter) with one mutex. Sensors that share an ADC share its lock too. Next ¶ Testing and CI shows how the adapter and driver are tested without hardware.

docs.text: Quickstart ¶ Read a temperature from your MCU: wire three pins, write a small ADC adapter, call two driver functions. 1. Wire it ¶ MCP9700 MCU Notes VDD 3.3 V (2.3 V to 5.5 V) 0.1 µF to 1 µF ceramic capacitor to GND, close to the pins GND GND Common with the ADC ground VOUT ADC input 100 mV to 1.75 V; the ADC range must reach 1.75 V Pin numbers depend on the package: SOT-23-3 and TO-92-3 are VDD 1, VOUT 2, GND 3. The Hardware page has the SC70-5 pinout, the output limits and the ADC settings. 2. Add the driver ¶ Add the repository as a submodule and link the hf::mcp9700 CMake target (or include inc/ and the generated version header, with C++17). Installation covers CMake and ESP-IDF. git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-mcp9700-driver.git external/hf-mcp9700-driver 3. Write the adapter ¶ The adapter is the only platform code. It brings the ADC up and returns the voltage at VOUT in volts. Replace the two platform_* calls with your SDK's. my_adc.hpp class MyAdc { public : // Bring the ADC up. The driver calls this from Initialize(); return true when it is ready. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_adc_init (); } return ready_ ; } // Volts at the MCP9700 VOUT pin. Return 0 on success, any other value on failure. int ReadChannelV ( uint8_t channel , float * voltage_v ) noexcept { int32_t mv = 0 ; if ( ! ready_ || ! platform_adc_read_mv ( channel , & mv )) { return 1 ; } * voltage_v = static_cast < float > ( mv ) / 1000.0F ; return 0 ; } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Return the voltage at the sensor pin , after your ADC's calibration and after undoing any divider or attenuator in front of it. Porting explains each method. 4. Read the temperature ¶ main.cpp #include "mcp9700_thermistor.hpp" int print_board_temperature ( MyAdc & adc ) { hf :: mcp9700 :: Mcp9700Thermistor < MyAdc > sensor ( & adc , /*adc_channel=*/ 0 ); // 500 mV at 0 °C, 10 mV/°C if ( ! sensor . Initialize ()) { // 1. brings the ADC up return -1 ; // adapter failed: ADC unit, channel, pin } float celsius = 0.0F ; if ( ! sensor . ReadTemperatureCelsius ( & celsius )) { // 2. one ADC read, (V - 0.5 V) / 0.01 V/°C return -2 ; // ADC error, or VOUT outside the sensor's range } std :: printf ( "Board temperature: %.1f C \n " , static_cast < double > ( celsius )); return 0 ; } What each step does: The constructor stores the adapter pointer, the channel and the default coefficients (500 mV at 0 °C, 10 mV/°C). It does not touch the ADC. Initialize() calls your adapter's EnsureInitialized() . Reads fail until it has returned true . ReadTemperatureCelsius() calls ReadChannelV() once and returns (V − 0.5) / 0.01 . A reading of 0.75 V is 25 °C. A result outside −40 °C to +125 °C by more than 8 °C (an open, grounded or shorted input) fails instead. This example is built by the host CI, so it compiles against the current headers. If it does not work ¶ Symptom First thing to check Initialize() returns false Your EnsureInitialized() : ADC unit, channel, pin Reads fail, LastError() is Error::kOutOfRange VOUT at 0 V (open wire, sensor unpowered, wrong ADC channel), at the supply, or the adapter returns millivolts Reads too high or too low by a fixed factor ADC full scale, attenuation or a divider not undone Off by a few degrees Sensor grade and the ADC's own error ( Transfer function ) Next ¶ API guide : calibration, averaging, error handling. Hardware : output characteristics, ADC resolution, layout. Examples : the ESP32-C6 application.

docs.text: Transfer function ¶ How the driver turns a voltage into a temperature, which coefficients it uses, and how large the errors are. The equation ¶ The datasheet characterises the sensor with a first-order transfer function (Equation 4-1): VOUT = TC × TA + V0°C The driver solves it for the temperature: T = (V − v_zero_c) / v_per_c v_zero_c is V 0°C , the output at 0 °C, and v_per_c is T C , the temperature coefficient, both in volts. The constants are in namespace hf::mcp9700 . They default to the datasheet's typical values and can be replaced per sensor ( Configuration ). Coefficient Default Constant v_zero_c 0.5 V kDefaultVoltsAtZeroC v_per_c 0.01 V/°C kDefaultVoltsPerCelsius Output over temperature ¶ Temperature (°C) V OUT , typical (V) −40 0.10 0 0.50 +25 0.75 +85 1.35 +125 1.75 These values follow from the typical coefficients. They do not depend on the supply voltage: the output is not ratiometric, and the line regulation is 0.1 °C/V typical. Where the error comes from ¶ Source Size What to do Sensor accuracy ±4 °C (MCP9700), ±2 °C (MCP9700A), 0 °C to +70 °C Choose the grade; calibrate ( Hardware ) Nonlinearity ±0.5 °C typical, 0 °C to +70 °C Left after a one-point calibration; AN1001 compensates it ADC offset and gain Depends on the MCU Calibrated ADC readings in the adapter ADC resolution 0.08 °C to 1 °C per code Choose the reference and range ( Hardware ) Noise Depends on the board Decoupling, averaging ( API guide ) A one-point calibration at +25 °C reduces the first row to ±0.5 °C typical between 0 °C and +70 °C (datasheet Section 4.1). Measuring a change relative to +25 °C is accurate to ±1 °C typical over the same range without any calibration. Limits of the model ¶ The driver applies the equation only inside the specified range plus a margin (−48 °C to +133 °C, 20 mV to 1.83 V by default). An open or grounded input (0 V, which would be −50 °C) and a shorted-to-supply input fail with Error::kOutOfRange instead of returning a temperature ( API guide ). The coefficients are fixed when you construct the object. To change them, construct a new one. There is no curve correction for the nonlinearity; the datasheet's AN1001 describes a lookup-table method. Next ¶ Configuration shows how to calibrate the coefficients; Hardware shows how to set up the ADC.

docs.title: Where the error comes from

docs.text: The driver applies the equation only inside the specified range plus a margin (−48 °C to +133 °C, 20 mV to 1.83 V by default). An open or grounded input (0 V, which would be −50 °C) and a shorted-to-supply input fail with Error::kOutOfRange instead of returning a temperature ( API guide ). The coefficients are fixed when you construct the object. To change them, construct a new one. There is no curve correction for the nonlinearity; the datasheet's AN1001 describes a lookup-table method.

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms you may see while bringing up an MCP9700, their causes and the fix for each. Start with a multimeter on VOUT: about 0.75 V at +25 °C, and compare it with ReadVoltage() . If the meter agrees with the temperature, the problem is in the ADC or the adapter; if it does not, it is in the wiring or the sensor. Build ¶ Symptom Cause and fix mcp9700_version.h not found The header was not generated. Link hf::mcp9700 , or include the settings file ( Installation ) No matching call to EnsureInitialized or ReadChannelV The adapter's methods are missing or differ. Match the contract ( Porting ) Initialisation and reads ¶ Symptom Cause and fix Initialize() returns false Null adapter, v_per_c not a finite positive number, v_zero_c not finite, or EnsureInitialized() failed. Check the arguments, then the ADC set-up Every read returns false Check LastError() . kNotInitialized : Initialize() not called or failed. kAdcError : ReadChannelV() returns non-zero; return 0 on success only and check the channel. kOutOfRange : see below Reads fail with kOutOfRange ReadVoltage() shows the raw VOUT. Outside 20 mV to 1.83 V (default range): open wire, grounded input, sensor unpowered or wrong pin (0 V); input shorted to VDD; adapter returns millivolts; or the part runs outside −40 °C to +125 °C ( Configuration ) Wrong temperature ¶ Symptom Cause and fix Wrong by a constant factor ADC full scale, attenuation or a divider not undone. Return volts at the pin ( Hardware ) A few degrees off, steady Sensor grade and ADC offset. Calibrate ( Configuration ) Warmer than the room The sensor follows the board, heated by nearby parts. Move it, or use TO-92 for air ( Hardware ) Noisy Supply noise or digital lines nearby. Decoupling, 200 Ω in VDD, averaging ( Hardware ) Wrong right after power-up from a GPIO Read before the turn-on time. Wait at least 800 µs, with margin ( Hardware ) Still stuck ¶ Open an issue with the MCU, the supply voltage, the ADC settings, a multimeter reading of VOUT and what the driver returned.

docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs hardfoc-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. Three layers, one of them yours ¶ Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one Mcp9700Thermistor object per sensor, whose public calls (listed from inc/mcp9700_thermistor.hpp) initialise the ADC and return degrees Celsius. The core turns one ADC voltage into a temperature with (V - v_zero_c) / v_per_c. The ADC adapter contract is the template parameter: any class with the two methods named in the header's documentation, checked at compile time. The platform port is the only code you write: that class, which brings your ADC up and returns the voltage at the sensor's VOUT pin. Below it is the hardware.
